query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a powder‐pack boriding surface treatment to boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment will create a dense, high-hardness boride layer that acts as a diffusion barrier and significantly enhances the component's resistance to molten aluminum corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based alloy surfaces (e.g., high-entropy alloy components currently used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment) without the optimized dense boride layer.
generation.intervention: Powder‐pack boriding treatment performed at elevated temperatures (e.g., 900–950 °C) for a controlled duration to develop a reinforced layer composed of MB-type and M2B-type borides.
generation.conditions: The treated components are exposed to molten aluminum under operational temperatures of hot-dip plating. The treatment effect is expected to remain effective under continuous molten exposure and typical thermal cycling encountered in industrial processes up to the temperature range used during treatment.
generation.structural_mediator: A reinforced surface layer consisting primarily of high-hardness MB-type and M2B-type borides that effectively reduces the diffusion pathways for aluminum into the substrate.
generation.mechanism: The powder‐pack boriding process induces inward boron diffusion and outward metal diffusion, forming a continuous, dense boride layer with a significant increase in microhardness. This layer serves as a barrier to molten aluminum, slowing its penetration and subsequent corrosive attack compared to untreated or conventionally-treated surfaces.
generation.predicted_outcome: Components receiving the optimized powder‐pack boriding treatment will exhibit a significantly lower corrosion rate (e.g., reduced weight loss and shallower corrosion depth) in molten aluminum compared to the baseline untreated components, thereby potentially extending service life.
generation.baseline: Untreated boride-based components or components with conventional surface treatments that do not form a continuous, high-hardness boride layer.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected under the controlled treatment conditions (temperature, duration, boron powder purity) and within the operational temperature range typical of hot-dip aluminum plating. Extreme thermal cycling or mechanical wear beyond typical operational limits may degrade the boride layer’s integrity.
generation.uncertainty: The precise treatment parameters (exact temperature, duration, and boron pack composition) needed to maximize corrosion resistance in a molten aluminum environment remain to be fully optimized, and variability in base alloy composition might alter the treatment efficacy.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment: one set undergoing the optimized powder‐pack boriding treatment (e.g., at 900–950 °C for a determined optimal time) and a control set receiving no such treatment. Subject both sets to identical molten aluminum immersion tests under simulated operational conditions (temperature, duration, and thermal cycling representative of industrial processes).
measurements: Surface microhardness and phase composition characterization (XRD, SEM) before and after testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the borided samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in corrosion rate, corrosion depth, or degradation of surface properties compared to the control set, then the hypothesis that powder‐pack boriding enhances molten-aluminum corrosion resistance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloys were treated by powder-pack boriding to improve their surface hardness and wear resistance. The variation of boriding layer thickness with time and temperature was studied. Then, the frequency factor D0 and diffusion activation energy Q of element B in HEA are calculated to be 9.15 × 10−5 m2/s and 206.93 kJ/mol, respectively. The diffusion behavior of elements in the boronizing process was investigated and shows that the boride layer forms with the metal atoms diffusing outward and the diffusion layer forms with the B atoms diffusing inward by the Pt-labeling method. In addition, the surface microhardness of CoCrFeNiMn HEA was significantly improved to 23.8 ± 1.4 Gpa, and the friction coefficient was reduced from 0.86 to 0.48~0.61.Keywords: high entropy alloy, boronizing, growth kinetics, boronizing mechanism, wear resistance

In this study, a reinforced layer was prepared on the surface of HEA by powder-pack boriding and focused on the effect of temperature and duration on the boronizing of CoCrFeNiMn HEA. The boronized samples were characterized using various methods. Furthermore, the properties of boronized CoCrFeNiMn alloys and diffusion behavior were investigated. This study could provide a reference for high hardness and high wear resistance HEA that could be used in a variety of industrial applications, such as the mold and crucible used in the cast aluminum industry [,], because the borides formed on the surface have high hardness, excellent corrosion resistance, and wear resistance [,], which allow HEA to be applied in special environments to increase service life.

Boronizing treatment was performed at 850, 900, and 950 °C for 3 h, 6 h, 9 h, 12 h, 15 h, and 18 h, respectively. The annealed CoCrFeNiMn samples were placed in the alumina crucible, then packed with high-purity boron powder. The alumina crucibles were tightly closed by a high-temperature sodium silicate and kaolin binder to make them airtight. After boriding was completed, the sealed crucible was extracted and air-cooled to room temperature, and the samples were ultrasonically cleaned using anhydrous ethanol to remove the boron powder from the surface.

In this work, a reinforced layer on the surface of HEA was successfully synthesized by powder-pack boriding. The microstructure, microhardness, wear resistance, and boriding mechanism were investigated. The following conclusions can be summarized: The microstructure of the surface layer is mainly composed of MB-type boride and M2B-type boride. The original interface of the surface layer is located at the interface between the BL and the diffusion layer, where element B diffuses inward and metal elements diffuse outward. The activation energy and frequency factor of the B element in CoCrFeMnNi HEA are 206.93 kJ/mol and 9.15 × 10−5 m2/s, respectively. Increasing the boronizing duration and temperature resulted in an increase in the BL and diffusion layer thickness. The surface strengthening of CoCrFeMnNi HEA was achieved by the boriding treatment. Its surface microhardness has significantly increased from 3.9 ± 0.1 Gpa to 23.8 ± 1.4 Gpa. The surface layer shows a lower friction coefficient of 0.48 than that of the substrate (0.86).
